sections.body:
A **greeting** is a small talk you use to say hello to somebody. Every conversation you ever have starts with one.

Hello is the easiest one. You can say hello at any time of day. It always works.

Sometimes you use a more exact word. You say **good morning** before lunch. You say **good afternoon** after lunch and before the sun goes down. You say **good evening** in the evening, when it is dark outside.

Then comes the second part: **introducing yourself**. That means telling somebody your name. *Hello, I am Minh.*

That is all a greeting really is. Two tiny pieces: a hello, and your name. After that you can talk about anything you like.

Greetings are also the friendliest part of a day. A shopkeeper greets you. A teacher greets you. A friend greets you on the playground. When you greet first, people feel welcome around you.

In this book you will learn which hello to use, how to say your name clearly, and what to do when you meet somebody you have never met before.
sections.heading: A greeting is how a talk begins

sections.body:
Different greetings are used at different times. That is all.

Hello works all day long. It is friendly and it is safe. Use hello when you are not sure.

Hi is a shorter, more casual hello. It is good with friends your own age.

Good morning is for the start of the day. You say it when the sun is still up and the day has just begun.

Good afternoon is for the middle of the day, after lunch.

Good evening is for the end of the day, when the lights come on.

Good night is different. It is not a hello. It is what you say before you sleep, or when you leave somebody at night.

And **goodbye** ends the talk. You say hello at the start and goodbye at the end. A whole small conversation can be just three words: *Hello. I am Minh. Goodbye.*

If you are unsure which one to use, use hello. It never sounds wrong.
examples: Good morning! Did you sleep well?
Good night, Dad. See you tomorrow.
sections.heading: Hello, hi, good morning and good night

sections.body:
Telling somebody your name is the easiest part of meeting them. You only need a few seconds.

The old way is the clearest way. You say your name twice. *Hello, I am Minh. My name is Minh.* Now the other person is sure.

You can also use **I am** and **my name is**. They mean the same thing. *I am Minh* is short and warm. *My name is Minh* is a little more formal.

Look at the person while you say it. Looking down at your shoes makes your voice small. Looking up makes it clear.

Smile while you say it. A smile does not change the words, but it changes how they land.

Then ask their name back. *Hello, I am Minh. What is your name?* Or *And what should I call you?* The second one is lovely with a teacher or an older person.

And if you forget to say your name, that is fine. Just say it a moment later. *Oh, I forgot. I am Minh.*
examples: Hello, I am Minh. My name is Minh.
My name is Lan, and this is my brother Bao.
Hello, I am Minh. What is your name?
sections.heading: Saying your name so people hear it

sections.body:
These are the greeting words. They are small, and they do a lot of work.

Hello is the word for greeting anybody at any time. It is the safest word you know.

Hi is the short, friendly version of hello. You use it with people you already know.

How are you? is a question you ask after the hello. The person usually answers *I am fine*, and the talk keeps going.

My name is tells somebody who you are. It is a little more careful than *I am*.

Nice to meet you is what you say when you meet somebody for the first time. It is polite and warm.

Goodbye ends the talk. You use it when you are leaving or when the other person is going away.

Learn these six and you can start a talk with anybody, anywhere.
sections.heading: The words you use when you meet somebody

terms.gloss: The word you say when you meet somebody. You can use it all day long.
A short and casual way to say hello, used with people you already know.

terms.example: Good morning! How are you today?
terms.gloss: A friendly question you ask after saying hello, to start a small talk.

terms.example: My name is Lan, and I am seven.
terms.gloss: The words you use to tell somebody your own name.

terms.example: Nice to meet you. I am Minh.
terms.gloss: What you say the first time you meet somebody. It is polite and warm.

sections.body:
Meeting a new person feels big. This small routine makes it easy.

First, walk over to the person. Stand close enough to talk.

Next, look at their face and smile.

Then say hello. Use the word that fits the time of day.

After that, say your name. Say it slowly enough to hear.

Then ask their name. Wait for the answer.

Then ask one small question. *How are you?* or *Do you like this game?* A question gives the other person something easy to answer.

Last, say goodbye when you go. *Goodbye, see you tomorrow!*

That is the whole thing. Seven small steps, and you did it.
examples: Nice to meet you. What is your name?
sections.heading: How to meet somebody new, step by step
steps: Walk over and stand near the person.
Look at their face and smile.
Say hello, and say it for the time of day.

sections.body:
Some children find greeting people difficult. That is normal. It gets easier with practice.

Start small. A nod and a wave is a hello too. So is a smile.

Practise at home first. Say hello to your family, to the mirror, to your cat. It gets easier.

If you are shy, stay close to a grown-up you know. Greetings are easier when somebody is beside you.

And if you meet somebody new, remember they were once new too. Grown-up strangers say hello to you because they want to be friendly. Say hello back, even in a small voice.

A quiet hello is still a hello. Say it, and it will come out louder next time.
examples: Hello. I am Minh. I am a bit shy.
sections.heading: When saying hello feels hard

item.summary: A greeting is how a conversation starts. After reading this you can say hello to grown-ups and friends, say your own name, and start a small talk with anybody you meet.
item.title: Saying Hello and Introducing Yourself
